newsitem.title: USA: Negotiator says tobacco talks near critical phase.
newsitem.headline: Negotiator says tobacco talks near critical phase.

text.p: Negotiations between cigarette makers and anti-smoking forces aimed at an industrywide settlement for damage claims and regulation are about to enter a critical phase, a participant said Monday.
"I think in the next two or three weeks we'll know if we're going to be able to work this thing out," said Mississippi Attorney General Michael Moore.
He spoke to reporters as he and counterparts from 23 other states met to discuss the status of the negotiations and where they should go from here.

Moore said Mississippi and other states that have sued tobacco companies to recover health care costs from smoking have been "empowered" by last week's federal court decision in North Carolina, which upheld the federal Food and Drug Administration's authority to regulate tobacco.
He said negotiations among the parties would probably resume sometime next week, although he declined to disclose the location.

Published reports have said the talks could result in the industry paying as much as $300 billion over 25 years into a compensation fund for smokers with lung cancer and other diseases. In return, cigarette makers would get broad protection from lawsuits.
Illinois Attorney General Jim Ryan told reporters the states would never agree "to blanket immunity," protecting the industry from future litigation.
"We're not going to bar the door," he said.
There have been reports that the negotiators were working on a possible cap on future individual health-related lawsuits against the tobacco companies should an overall settlement be reached.

Mississippi's Moore said the talks to date have centred on public health and children's issues and that money will be discussed later. He said "great progress" had been made on possible marketing and advertising restrictions for all age groups.

Asked what he hoped the industry would eventually give up, Moore said, "everything that has been proposed in the FDA guideline, everything. Plus we'll get a ban on all outdoor advertising, kill the Marlboro man, kill Joe Camel, get rid of the vending machines, get rid of Internet advertising, get rid of point-of-sale advertising.
"We're going to shoot for it all ... and then tightly regulate the industry," Moore said.
In last week's court decision, the FDA's proposal to curb certain kinds of advertising and promotional material was rejected by the court.

Moore said a final resolution of the appeals from the North Carolina decision may be two or more years away but suggested the industry is facing pressure to resolve matters across the board earlier than that because several states, including his own, are in court seeking hefty damages in lawsuits that are about to go to trial.

"If we try our case in Mississippi in July and if we win, if Florida wins in August and Texas wins in September, what shape is the tobacco industry going to be in financially after three states have hit them hard?" he asked.

"Rather than put the tobacco industry in bankruptcy ... what we're trying to do is make sure we have some progress here, that we really do reduce teenaged smoking and really, fundamentally change the way the tobacco companies do business," he said.
